footer.tagline: First-time cross-country glamping, one off-grid stop at a time

hero.title: cross-country glamping run, documented honestly
hero.subtitle: We quit pretending we knew what we were doing, hitched an off-grid camper to a pickup truck, and drove across the country. This is the story of the truck, the camper, the dog, and the two of us who are still figuring it out.

story.title: Zero glamping experience. One very big truck. No real plan.
story.paragraph1: Neither of us had spent more than a weekend in a tent before we decided the right move was a multi-week, coast-leaning trip in a camper we had owned for exactly eleven days. We told our families it was a long vacation. It was actually a crash course in propane, solar math, and arguing about backing up a trailer.
story.paragraph2: The truck is a Ford F350, which felt enormous in our driveway and suddenly felt correctly sized the first time we hit a crosswind in Wyoming. Behind it rides an MGC 16 XTC, a rugged off-grid teardrop-style camper with its own battery bank, water tank, and just enough room for two adults, one dog, and far too much camping gear.
story.paragraph3: We are not experts. We are not influencers with a sponsorship deck. We are two first-timers writing down what actually happened at each stop, including the parts where we got something wrong, so the next nervous beginner has a more honest map than we did.
story.pullQuote: We didn't learn to glamp before we left. We learned by doing it badly in a parking lot in Nebraska, then slightly less badly every night after.

hero.title: First Stop: The Badlands Taught Us What Off-Grid Really Means
hero.subtitle: Day three of our first cross-country run in the Ford F-350 and MGC 16 XTC, and the Badlands already rewired how we think about camping without hookups.
hero.author: Written by the RVV Camping crew
hero.imageAlt: Ford F-350 with MGC 16 XTC truck camper parked at a Badlands National Park overlook at sunrise

content.intro: We left the driveway with a full water tank, a half-finished packing list, and a mix of confidence and nerves that only a first off-grid trip can produce. Four states and one National Park later, the Badlands handed us our first real lesson in what this rig, and this way of traveling, is actually capable of.

sections.heading: Leaving the Driveway
sections.body: We had spent two months prepping for this. Spreadsheets, checklists, a dry run in the backyard. None of it fully prepared us for the quiet that sets in about three hours into a real trip, when the town behind you disappears and it is just the highway, the hum of the diesel, and a camper full of gear you hope you packed correctly.

sections.heading: The Ford F-350 Meets the MGC 16 XTC
sections.body: The pairing felt oversized on paper, a heavy-duty dually under a flatbed off-grid camper built for serious remoteness. On the road it settled in fast. The XTC's long-range tanks and solar setup meant we skipped two planned fuel-and-water stops entirely, and the suspension soaked up the washboard gravel leading into the park without a single rattle from the cabinets.
sections.imageAlt: Ford F-350 towing the MGC 16 XTC off-grid camper down a gravel road toward the Badlands

sections.heading: First Night Off the Grid
sections.body: No hookups, no neighbors, no cell signal past a single flickering bar. We ran the induction cooktop off the camper's battery bank, boiled water for coffee at sunset, and sat on the tailgate watching the rock formations turn from gold to rust to a deep, bruised purple. It was the first time either of us had camped somewhere this isolated, and it was quieter than we knew how to process.

sections.heading: Badlands at Golden Hour
sections.body: Every guidebook warns you about the light here, and every guidebook undersells it. The striped buttes catch the early sun in bands of pink and ochre that shift by the minute. We set an alarm for 5:15 a.m. on day two just to catch it from the Door Trail overlook, and it was worth every bit of the lost sleep.
sections.imageAlt: Striped rock formations in Badlands National Park glowing pink and gold at sunrise

sections.heading: What We'd Do Differently
sections.body: We underestimated how much dust gets into everything out here, and we will pack a second set of cabin air filters next time. We also learned to top off water at every reasonable chance rather than waiting for the tank to run low. Small lessons, but exactly the kind you only learn by actually going.

stops.name: Badlands
stops.description: Our shakedown stop. First night running the MGC's solar and water systems for real, parked on BLM land just outside the park with the striped buttes glowing at sunset.
highlights: Free dispersed camping on Sage Creek Rim Road, no hookups needed
Sunrise light on the formations is worth the early alarm
Last reliable cell signal before Wyoming, download your maps here

stops.name: Black Hills
stops.description: Slower pace through the Black Hills National Forest, running the generator just enough to keep the fridge happy while we hiked and let the truck cool down after the first long haul.
highlights: Forest service roads had room for the camper with no reservations
Good spot to flush and refill the MGC's fresh water tank in town
Cooler nights meant barely touching the furnace

stops.name: Yellowstone
stops.description: The longest stay of the trip. Split between a paid campground for laundry and tank dumps, and two nights boondocking near the park's east entrance for quiet and dark skies.
highlights: Book shoulder-season campsites months ahead, they fill fast
Bear-proof storage is mandatory, plan your camper's exterior space for it
East entrance pullouts had the best stargazing of the whole route

stops.name: Grand Teton
stops.description: A short, scenic leg mostly spent just looking at the mountains. Easiest tow of the trip, flat roads and the camper barely noticed the grade.
highlights: Jenny Lake turnouts are tight, scout parking before towing in
Quick stop for propane refill at the gateway town
Clear mornings gave the best mountain reflections on the lake

stops.name: Moab
stops.description: Where the off-grid build finally earned its keep. Five nights on slickrock BLM land outside Arches, running entirely on solar and the onboard water tank.
highlights: BLM land along Willow Springs Road had the best sunset views
Sand and grit are rough on seals, rinse the undercarriage after
A dedicated water filter made boondocking this long comfortable

stops.name: Grand Canyon
stops.description: The finale. Desert View campground for two nights, then a long detour to the North Rim for the quieter overlooks before heading home.
highlights: North Rim closes earlier in the season, call ahead before detouring
Desert heat meant running the roof fan nonstop, pack extra battery
Fewer crowds at the North Rim made it the trip's best overlook

hero.title: A Ford F-350 and an MGC 16 XTC, built for places without hookups
hero.subtitle: Everything we drive, tow, and live out of on this trip. Here's the full rundown of the truck, the camper, and the gear that keeps us off-grid.

rigOverview.title: One heavy-duty truck, one off-grid camper, zero regrets
rigOverview.paragraph1: The Ford F-350 is a diesel dually we picked specifically for towing capacity and stability, not comfort. It felt enormous in our driveway and exactly right the first time a crosswind hit us in Wyoming. It's the kind of truck that makes a 2,000-pound camper feel like an afterthought on the highway.
rigOverview.paragraph2: Behind it rides the MGC 16 XTC, a rugged off-grid truck camper with its own battery bank, fresh water tank, and solar array, built for exactly the kind of boondocking we're doing. It's compact enough to handle forest service roads and slickrock, with just enough room for two adults, one dog, and far too much gear.

image.alt: Ford F-350 towing an MGC 16 XTC off-grid camper on a highway

specs.title: The specs that make off-grid possible
specs.subtitle: What's actually powering, hauling, and housing us for six weeks on the road.

items.title: Diesel power and towing capacity
items.description: The F-350's diesel engine and dually axle give us well over the towing capacity we need for the fully loaded XTC, with margin to spare on mountain grades.

items.title: Battery bank and power management
items.description: The camper's onboard lithium battery bank keeps the fridge, lights, and induction cooktop running for days without needing a hookup or generator.

items.title: Fresh water and tank capacity
items.description: A sizable fresh water tank gets us through four to five days of cooking, dishes, and quick showers before we need to refill in town.

items.title: Sleeps two, comfortably
items.description: The XTC's layout fits two adults and a dog without feeling like a tent, with real storage instead of gear piled on the floor.

items.title: Rooftop solar array
items.description: Solar panels on the camper roof keep the battery bank topped off on sunny days, which out west has been most of them.

items.title: Heavy-duty suspension and all-terrain tires
items.description: Upgraded suspension and all-terrain tires on both the truck and camper have handled washboard gravel and slickrock without a single flat so far.

gearList.title: Essential gear riding along with us
gearList.subtitle: The equipment that actually earns its space in the truck bed and camper storage.

items.title: Recovery gear
items.description: Traction boards, a shovel, and a basic tow strap for the soft sand and mud we didn't always see coming.

items.title: Portable power station
items.description: A backup battery pack for charging phones, cameras, and laptops when we don't want to dip into the camper's main bank.

items.title: Camp cooking setup
items.description: A two-burner propane stove, cast iron skillet, and the camper's built-in induction cooktop cover most of what we cook.

items.title: Water filtration system
items.description: A gravity-fed filter lets us top off from streams or questionable spigots without worrying about what's in the tank.

items.title: Camp furniture
items.description: Two folding chairs, a collapsible table, and a dog bed that Biscuit has claimed as permanently hers.

items.title: Tool kit and spare parts
items.description: Basic hand tools, extra fuses, hitch hardware, and a tire repair kit, because something always needs tightening after a gravel road.

faq.title: Living with the rig, honestly
faq.subtitle: What people ask us most at gas stations and campgrounds.

items.question: How often does the rig need maintenance on a trip like this?
items.answer: We check tire pressure and fluid levels every few days and do a full inspection weekly. Washboard roads and elevation changes mean small issues show up fast if you're not looking.

items.question: Is the F-350 overkill for the MGC 16 XTC?
items.answer: On paper, maybe. In practice, the extra towing margin has made mountain passes, headwinds, and loaded gear feel like a non-issue instead of a stress point.

items.question: What was the biggest surprise about living out of the camper?
items.answer: How livable it actually is. We expected to feel cramped after a week. Six weeks in, the layout, storage, and battery setup have held up better than we did.
